QF.id: SIA Assessment Frameworks Techniques and Standards_24

question.text: Which statement BEST describes the rationale for combining qualitative and quantitative data in an SIA engagement?

answer.text: Quantitative methods are always superior because numbers don't lie
Qualitative methods are always superior because they capture real stories
Quantitative data analyses large numerical data while qualitative research reveals broader, in-depth effects, and combining them helps validate and interpret SIA evidence
Combining qualitative and quantitative data is discouraged because it creates inconsistent reporting

explanation.text: The Logic: Data may be available in both qualitative and quantitative forms. Quantitative research analyses large numerical data, while qualitative research reveals broader, in-depth effects, and tools such as FGDs can validate quantitative beneficiary data. Using both forms together helps interpret SIA evidence more reliably than using either alone. The Trap: Neither method is universally superior; each has limits, especially with softer outcomes. Combining qualitative and quantitative data is supported, not discouraged, in SIA practice. Note: Pair quantitative indicators with qualitative corroboration such as beneficiary interviews, FGD notes, or community feedback so that observations from one source are checked against the other.
